newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lufthansa union to consider strike ballot.
newsitem.headline: Lufthansa union to consider strike ballot.

text.p: The German union leading worker protests against airline Deutsche Lufthansa AG in a long-running pay dispute said on Tuesday it would consider whether to ballot for full strikes early next year.

DAG, which shares representation of the airline's some 50,000 staff with the OeTV public sector and transport union, has already led two limited walk-outs by the airline's staff costing it some 30 million marks ($19.4 million).
But an all-out strike would have potentially much more damaging consequences for the airline than the two protests to date, which under labour law have been limited to a maximum of two hours each.

A DAG spokesman said after a meeting of its wage committee on Tuesday that no further protests were planned but that it would discuss whether to ballot workers on an all-out strike at its first meeting in January.
"That would be for a proper strike without any time limit," the spokesman said by telephone.
He added that if the ballot produced a majority of 70 percent of DAG members in favour, a strike could go ahead immediately.

DAG says that in negotiations Lufthansa has not offered its members a 1997 wage increase anywhere near in line with others in the industry. The union is seeking a 1997 wage rise of around four percent.

It is also angry that Lufthansa wants the new contracts to last 27 months instead of a year. Given the threat that many Lufthansa jobs could be moved abroad, the union would not tie itself to a two-year contract, DAG has said.

A two-hour stoppage last Thursday by around 1,500 flight-crew members and aircraft technicians cost Lufthansa about 20 million marks as it had to cancel some 92 European flights, hitting around 6,500 passengers.
The walk-outs affected Lufthansa's main hub in Frankfurt as well as Munich, Berlin, Hamburg and Duesseldorf.
The German airline has called for DAG to stop the industrial action and come back to the negotiating table.

But Lufthansa, under increasing price pressure from rivals seeking to gain an entry into the lucrative German market, is known to be seeking deep cost reductions over the coming years. ($ = 1.545 German Marks)
